title: Notes d'épigraphie (BEFEO 15, 1915): Inscription de Vó-canh
venue: Bulletin de l'École française d'Extrême-Orient 15 (via Angkor Database PDF)
ask_addressed: Southeast Asia: transmission of Sanskrit, Hindu-Buddhist religion and Indian scripts (Pallava-derived) to Funan, Champa, Java, Cambodia. Primary: Vo Canh inscription, Kutai Yupa inscriptions, Angkor-period Sanskrit inscriptions (Cœdès, Finot, Majumdar translations), Chinese envoy accounts (Kang Tai and Zhu Ying on Funan in the Liang shu or Nan Qi shu).
quote: L'esprit du grand Açoka revit dans cet édit.
summary: Finot's catalogue entry gives the damaged Sanskrit stele of Vo Canh (Khanh Hoa), in vasantatilaka metre, with a French rendering of the legible last lines: a king of the line of Sri Mara dedicates his treasure to the welfare of creatures. Finot argues the ideas (impermanence, compassion, giving) are Buddhist.
limits: Finot's own OCR text is noisy and the early lines are illegible. The Buddhist reading is Finot's interpretation, not stated in the text, and he refers dating to Bergaigne (not opened). Kingdom (Champa, Funan or Lam Ap) is not stated by the stele. Verifier: the quoted words are Finot's commentary comparing the edict to Asoka's, not the inscription's own wording, so kind is secondary and the Sanskrit-transfer strand is only inferred; the catalogue entry (opened) confirms Sanskrit, vasantatilaka metre and a king of Sri Mara's line, but gives no date (refers to Bergaigne, ISCC p. 191). The 200-500 CE range had no source and is nulled (composition 'not dated here'; strand start/end null). Title corrected to the printed 'Notes d'épigraphie'; DOI is printed on the PDF.

strand.what: Sanskrit verse edict with Buddhist-sounding ideas of compassion and giving, issued by a descendant of Sri Mara

title: The Yupa Inscriptions of King Mulavarman, from Koetei (East Borneo): Inscription A

quote: His were three eminent sons resembling the three sacrificial fires.
summary: Vogel's transcript and English translation of Yupa A: the king Mulavarman, son of Asvavarman and grandson of 'the great Kundunga', performed a Bahusuvarnaka sacrifice, the post being prepared by 'the chief amongst the twice-borns'. Pure Sanskrit verse (anustubh) on a sacrificial post, in Borneo.
limits: Translation is Vogel's, with footnotes noting Kern's alternative readings. The text names Brahmanical sacrifice and priests, but not how the practice reached Kutai; Kundunga's name is not Sanskrit and the dating is palaeographic only. Verifier: the quoted lines show Brahmanical sacrificial vocabulary in Borneo, not a transfer or its source; 'South India' origin is Vogel's palaeographic inference, so directness lowered from documented to inferred. Dates widened to 301-500 as Vogel gives them.

quote: it is undoubtedly the archaic type of the ancient Grantha character
summary: Vogel concludes the Kutai script is most closely related to the archaic Grantha used by early Pallava rulers, and ranks the early records Bhadravarman (Champa), Mulavarman, Purnavarman with c. 50 years between each, so Pallava-derived script is inferred from letter forms, not from a documented route.
limits: Palaeography cannot date closely or show the route; Vogel himself says the chronology 'stand[s] on no very firm ground' and notes no stone records exist from early Pallava India for comparison. Verifier: the quote drops Vogel's hedge: the sentence continues that this script 'appears to be most closely related' to the Koetei characters; also Vogel notes Pallava stone inscriptions only begin in the 7th century.

title: Hundian and Suwu: Suwu's mission to Tianzhu
venue: NII repository PDF (journal not printed on the pages read)

quote: it demonstrates that there had been little contact between Funan and Tianzhu prior to that time
summary: From the Liang shu and Kang Tai accounts of the Funan prince Suwu's trip to India and the Indian envoys Chen and Song, Fukami infers little earlier Funan-India contact and a state formed within Southeast Asia, so Indian contact is documented for c. 220s-240s, not before.

summary: Vickery argues that Hun-t'ien's date (1st century) is too early for Indianization and that the Funanese themselves did not claim acquaintance with India then; he calls the idea of Indian influence arriving with brahmans and a 'Hindu civilization implanted' 'early Southeast Asian academic folklore', and cites Manguin that Indianization followed about a millennium of steady exchange.

title: Beyond Indianization: Buddhist Knowledge Circulation in South and Southeast Asia
venue: Journal of Buddhist Studies and Applied Buddhism (JSBA) 11(3), pp. 737-755
ask_addressed: Include sceptical or alternative scholarship on 'Indianization' (Wolters, Mabbett, Hall) and what is documented versus inferred.
quote: Such a framework can obscure the historical agency of Southeast Asian societies in selecting, transforming, and circulating cultural and religious knowledge.
summary: A 2026 integrative review rejects one-way 'Indianization' in favour of multidirectional circulation and localization of Buddhist knowledge; it also concedes that two of its own cases remain speculative.
limits: A literature review of secondary work, not new evidence; the authors admit the lack of definitive empirical evidence for their two cases.
